**Claim:** Yes, there must exist an integer $N$ such that $K \subset K_N$.

**Proof.**

Since $K_n \subset \operatorname{int}(K_{n+1})$ for every $n$, we have
$$\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} K_n \subset \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{int}(K_{n+1}) = \bigcup_{n=2}^{\infty} \operatorname{int}(K_n) \subset \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{int}(K_n).$$
(The last inclusion holds because we simply add the non-negative set $\operatorname{int}(K_1)$.) Combined with the reverse inclusion $\operatorname{int}(K_n) \subset K_n$, which gives $\bigcup_n \operatorname{int}(K_n) \subset \bigcup_n K_n$, we obtain
$$\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{int}(K_n) = X.$$

Thus $\{\operatorname{int}(K_n)\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is an open cover of $X$, and in particular an open cover of the compact set $K \subset X$.

By compactness of $K$, there exists a finite subcover: indices $n_1, \dots, n_j$ with
$$K \subset \operatorname{int}(K_{n_1}) \cup \cdots \cup \operatorname{int}(K_{n_j}).$$
Set $N = \max\{n_1, \dots, n_j\}$. Since the sets $K_n$ are nested upward (each $K_n \subset \operatorname{int}(K_{n+1}) \subset K_{n+1}$, so $K_n \subset K_m$ whenever $n \le m$), each $\operatorname{int}(K_{n_i}) \subset K_{n_i} \subset K_N$. Hence
$$K \subset \operatorname{int}(K_{n_1}) \cup \cdots \cup \operatorname{int}(K_{n_j}) \subset K_N.$$

Therefore such an $N$ exists. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
